newsitem.title: FRANCE: SOCCER-FIFA HINT AT COMPROMISE OVER WORLD CUP FENCES.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-FIFA HINT AT COMPROMISE OVER WORLD CUP FENCES.

text.p: FIFA general secretary Sepp Blatter said for the first time on Tuesday he was optimistic that a solution could be found to the problem over perimeter fences at the World Cup finals in France next year.

While not going as far as saying that the fences would be removed from the stadiums, as FIFA would like, he did say: "I am very optimistic that the tall, 2.2 metre high fences could be lowered, and I am even hopeful that at some of the stadiums, they could be removed altogether.
"I am more hopeful now that a practical and human solution can be found to the problem. I know, for example, that the Mayor of Montpellier is confident the problem can be solved there."
Blatter was speaking exactly a year to the day before France 98 kicks off with matches in the new Stade de France at Saint Denis, just north of Paris, and Montpellier.

FIFA have been at odds with the previous French Government over the question of fencing fans in at the World Cup, citing last year's European championships in England as an event that went off without major trouble inside the stadiums, none of which were fenced.
"This has nothing to do with the change of government in France but the government, of course, has an influence," Blatter said. "But in France the will of the mayor ultimately decides the issue.

"Fences give the wrong global image for football. People are not animals and they don't need to be caged. Look at what happened last year in Guatemala when there was a catastrophe and 80 people died. Fences are not just a problem for France but a global problem."

That disaster, at the Stadio Mateo Flores in Guatemala City on October 25 last year was caused by over-crowding and fans being fenced in and there were harrowing similarities to the Hillsborough disaster in England in April 1989 which claimed 96 lives.
Still, Blatter admitted that FIFA would be powerless to act if fences are not removed.
"There is nothing we can do, the matches would go on, the spectators would still come, but the image of football would not look good."

Ten venues are being used next summer -- and there seemed to be some confusion over exactly how many were fenced or partly-fenced. While Blatter and Michel Platini, the joint-president of the organising committee said three stadiums had fences, a France '98 spokesman said he believed they all did.
The organising committee headed by Platini and his joint-president Fernand Sastre, reported that everything else was running as smoothly as possible.
Platini reported that ticket sales were a great success, with 1.27 million of the total of 2.5 million already sold in France.

Tickets for abroad would go on sale at the beginning of next year with more than half-a-million tickets on sale for less than 150 francs ($26). The cheapest tickets for the opening match will be on offer at 200 francs, and for the final at 350 francs.
"Everything is going to plan," said Platini. "All the stadiums will be ready by their deadlines and I am very optimistic."
Blatter added: "Looking at how the Tournoi de France has been organised this week I am optimistic that the World Cup in France next year will be a huge success."
